transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-03-05 15:00 UTC
Duration: 55 minutes
Attendees: Samantha Lee (Redwood AE), Marco Hernandez (Redwood SE), Daniel Park (Aurora CTO), Priya Rao (Lead ML Eng), Marcus Li (SRE)

Summary (auto-gen, may be rough):
Aurora is looking to move latency-critical agents to a dedicated pool; current hosted solutions are hitting P95 problems during peak hours. They want isolation for compliance, burst up to ~3x normal traffic during earnings calls, and deterministic latency around 150-300ms p95 for short completion tasks. Questions about KV cache persistence, quantization tradeoffs and fallback to hosted were raised.

Transcript:
[00:00] Samantha: hey everyone, thanks for joining - i'm sam from redwood, and with me is marco, our solutions eng. how's the morning daniel?
[00:07] Daniel: hey sam, good thanks. bit of background - we've been running on a managed hosted api for a year, but during end-of-month flows our latency spikes and that affects agent response times, so we're looking at reserved capacity options.
[00:18] Priya: yep, we need predictable throughput and isolation for sensitive PII workflows. also want to understand how burst capacity would work.
[00:25] Marco: cool, thanks. to confirm, you're evaluating dedicated reserved gpus vs hosted or private?
[00:30] Daniel: mostly dedicated, with private (vpc) as a backup for some regulated flows. hosted is attractive for quick ops but we need guaranteed performance.
[00:40] Samantha: perfect, we'll cover sizing, burst, vpc/private options, security and pricing. quick question - what's your current traffic shape? RPS, sequence lengths, that sort of thing.
[00:48] Priya: average 120 requests per second during normal hours, P95 hits 260 during peaks; sequence lengths vary, most are short - like 16 to 64 tokens, but a small percentage of long synths up to 512 tokens.
[01:05] Marco: okay that distribution is good to know. Dedicated pools are efficient for short sequences because of KV cache behavior; we can keep latency low with continuous batching. but bursts are interesting - do you have spikes that are sustained or short-lived?
[01:17] Marcus: spikes are usually short, like 30-90 minutes for specific events, but they can be big - roughly 3x baseline.
[01:24] Marco: we generally recommend a steady baseline reserved capacity sized for expected daily peak, plus configured burst capacity - for Redwood Dedicated that can be handled via burst nodes or autoscale policies depending on contract. bursts can be pre-warmed or allowed as short-term burstable instances; pricing differs.
[01:39] Daniel: okay how does the pre-warm work - do we need to commit?
[01:42] Samantha: pre-warm usually requires additional reservation or a short-term burst pool that's billed differently. simple way is a baseline reserve for normal peaks and enable burst for those known events. we'll send a sizing sheet with options.
[01:55] Priya: another thing - data isolation and encryption. we need KMS integration and audit logs; can Redwood Dedicated be in our VPC?
[02:04] Marco: yes, Redwood Private gives you a customer-managed control plane and VPC peering for private deployments; for Dedicated we have VPC options for dedicated customers - you can bring your VPC or use private endpoints. KMS/HSM integration is supported for key wrapping, and audit logs are available via the console or webhooks.
[02:22] Priya: nice. are audit logs SOC2-ready? we have an external audit process.
[02:27] Samantha: Redwood is SOC 2 compliant; we can share our attestation and the compliance pack. we'll attach it to the follow-up.
[02:34] Daniel: what about failover - if our dedicated pool saturates, can requests fall back to hosted?
[02:39] Marco: yes - smart routing policies can failover to hosted or to compatible model variants. note there's potential for latency change and different SLAs. Also model variant compatibility matters if you use quantized models for cost.
[02:52] Marcus: speaking of quantization, what's the tradeoff? we care about quality for user-facing agents.
[02:59] Marco: quantization gives large cost and throughput wins; for many models we recommend int8/4 pathways. but quality regression must be measured - Redwood Optimize helps recommend quant profiles per workload and we link that to evals. if you're very quality-sensitive, you can keep a higher-precision variant in the pool for critical flows.
[03:17] Priya: any real numbers for latency? we need p95 under 300ms for sub-64 tokens.
[03:22] Marco: on modern GPU instances with optimized kernels we typically see 80-180ms p95 for short sequences with continuous batching. exact numbers depend on model and seq length. we'll run a benchmark with your prompts to confirm.
[03:33] Daniel: good. do you have per-token pricing for Dedicated? how does reserved pricing compare to hosted?
[03:38] Samantha: pricing is a mix - reserved capacity is a monthly commitment for nodes; you get better unit economics the more you commit. hosted is usage-based per token/embedding. we'll send a pricing matrix showing breakpoints and burst charges.
[03:50] Priya: ok timeline - we want to pilot in Q2 and ramp to prod by end of Q3 if benchmarks look good.
[03:56] Samantha: that's reasonable. pilot usually starts with a short reserved pool and a benchmark run; we can do canary route traffic and then scale.
[04:04] Marco: want to dig into infra constraints - what cloud, network egress concerns, or regulatory regions?
[04:10] Daniel: we're primarily on AWS, multi-account. data residency for EU customers is a requirement for some products.
[04:16] Marco: we support region pinning and can run Dedicated in specific cloud regions; for VPC/on-prem private we can work through network setup. we'll need Marcus to coordinate on network egress rules and peering.
[04:28] Marcus: yep, we'll need a network diagram; also curious about storage of KV cache - is it ephemeral? do you persist cache across restarts?
[04:36] Marco: KV cache is in-memory per serving instance for latency; there's optional persistent cache layers for certain workloads but generally it's ephemeral. for long-lived sessions we do prefix caching strategies to reduce recomputation. sometimes docs transcribe that as "KV cash" - apologies for the quirks in auto transcripts.
[04:52] Priya: cool. about autoscaling - how fast can you scale up? is there cold-start latency?
[04:58] Marco: autoscale is policy driven. warm pools reduce cold start. scaling across GPUs does have some ramp time (tens of seconds to a few minutes depending on model load and pre-warm), so for very spiky events we recommend pre-warm or keeping buffer capacity.
[05:11] Daniel: if we do burst nodes, what's the SLA?
[05:14] Samantha: burst nodes are subject to availability; committed baseline has SLA-backed uptime and latency targets. we can document the details in the SLS and contract.
[05:23] Priya: security question - SAML/SSO for console, RBAC for team access?
[05:28] Marco: yes SAML/SSO, SCIM provisioning, and role-based controls. you can restrict routes and model access per team.
[05:35] Marcus: one more thing - do you expose token-level cost breakdowns and per-route dashboards?
[05:40] Samantha: yes that's in Redwood Console - token cost, latency per model, trace links and error analysis. very helpful for ops.
[05:47] Daniel: ok that's useful. last thing: who else from your side should we include for technical deep dive?
[05:52] Marco: myself and one infra eng, plus a solutions architect for network design if you want VPC. we'll coordinate dates.
[05:59] Samantha: great. recap of next steps - i'll send pricing/sizing and SOC2 docs; marco will draft benchmark plan and we'll schedule a deep dive with marcus. daniel/priya will send traffic profiles and sample prompts.
[06:12] Priya: sounds good. any blockers we should flag?
[06:16] Daniel: none immediate, just internal procurement will want the numbers.
[06:20] Samantha: understood, we'll accelerate the paperwork. thanks everyone.
[06:25] Daniel: thanks all.
